prize_parts.citation: for an oeuvre that remakes the boundaries between lyric, essay, narrative and drama through a lifelong dialogue with the classical tradition

statement.case_for: My first choice is unchanged, but I hold it with a narrower and more explicit argument than in round 1. The chair asked which works carry the whole-oeuvre case beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox. From public knowledge, and not from verified reading of the full corpus, I would point to Eros the Bittersweet, Plainwater, Men in the Off Hours, The Beauty of the Husband, Decreation, Antigonick, Red Doc> and Norma Jeane Baker of Troy. They span essay, lyric sequence, verse-novel, elegy and stage text. What recurs is a method: old Greek and later texts are reopened to ask how inherited forms carry present feeling, grief and desire. The same voice, dry and exact and then suddenly exposed, is recognisable in all of them. That is the argument for architecture over a string of experiments, and it speaks to distinctiveness of voice, formal achievement and sustained quality over several decades. I would rest the case on the verbal, narrative and lyric achievement, with book-object form as a secondary feature. I would also drop translation from the citation. It is not among the genres listed for this entry, and I do not want to credit it as a separate achievement. It stays as context for the classical dialogue. After the exchange, the tests colleagues set for the other leading candidates (later decades for Adonis, late volumes for Cărtărescu) are as unresolved as the one set for Carson. They do not show that her case is weaker.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot remove is that the evidence for breadth is thinner than the evidence for peak. Several members, Sward, Olsson, Sem-Sandberg and Mattson, ask whether the oeuvre is a consistent architecture or a series of brilliant experiments. My answer is an argument from a recurring method, not a demonstration across the whole corpus. Book-object and performance-oriented works are hard to judge as literature from text alone. Reception is concentrated in Anglophone literary culture, and the classical learning on which much of the work leans narrows its address. A committee reading in several languages may therefore judge her unevenly. I have also moved Adonis higher in my own estimation since round 1. Olsson's and Sward's argument that a language-level renewal is a more durable kind of distinctiveness is a serious one, and I cannot answer it from the evidence available to me.

responses.point: Sward ranks Carson fifth. She doubts that the hybrid and book-object works can be fairly assessed from translations, and she asks what in Carson's body of work beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox shows sustained development. She also asks that the Anglophone concentration of reception be weighed.
responses.response: This is the question I most needed to answer, and I have tried to in the case above. The development I see runs from the essayistic Eros the Bittersweet, through the verse-novel Autobiography of Red, to the elegiac Nox and the later returns to Greek drama and myth in Antigonick and Norma Jeane Baker of Troy. The method stays constant while the forms change, and I read that as development, not repetition. I concede that this is public knowledge and not verified reading, and I accept your point on reception. I would add one reply to your argument about access. If the Academy accepts that limit for poets in less widely read languages, it should also accept that Anglophone concentration is not by itself a literary weakness. Both limits call for careful reading, not for discounting. The book-object problem is real, and it is why I weight the verbal work over the object form.

responses.point: Olsson says Carson's strongest effects depend on the book as an object and on classical learning. He argues that breadth and durability are therefore harder to establish for her than for a poet whose achievement lies in the language itself. He asks which part of her work is most secure beyond the two named books.
responses.response: I take the force of this, and I answer it in two parts. The most secure parts, in my view, are the lyric and narrative verse of Autobiography of Red and the essay-poems of Plainwater and Decreation, where the achievement is in sentences and lineation, not in the object. If the book-object works were removed, I think the case would still stand, though it would be narrower. I do not claim that her achievement is language-level in your sense, since she renews a way of joining forms more than the idiom of a tradition. That is a real difference of kind, and I would not call it a difference of merit. Your argument has moved me to hold Adonis as a closer alternative than I did in round 1. I still cannot say that the object-dependence objection outweighs the translation-dependence objection against him.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg holds that Cărtărescu's long-form coherence is stronger evidence of architecture than Carson's hybrid and book-object forms. He says self-reference is a fault only if individual books stop discovering anything new, and that this should be tested book by book.
responses.response: I accept your book-by-book test, and I would apply it to Carson as well: does each of her major books find something its predecessors did not? I think Autobiography of Red, Nox and Antigonick do, but I cannot demonstrate it here. I accept your point that long-form coherence is easier to see in Cărtărescu. My own reservation, excess and repetition within the largest works, is still open, because you and Mattson both say you cannot settle the question of the late volumes. The condition under which I said I would move toward him has therefore not been met. I keep him as my first alternative and could support him as a final recommendation, but I do not move to him on the strength of an argument that is untested.

responses.point: Mattson did not rank Carson. She is unsure how much of the achievement lies in hybrid and book-object forms that translation cannot carry, and how much in the breadth of the oeuvre beyond a few well-known works. She says she would reconsider if I could name works that show sustained quality.
responses.response: I have named those works above, and I would ask you to test them rather than accept them. I would separate the questions you combine. The essays and lyric sequences are text-borne and can be assessed in translation. The book-object works cannot, and I would give them less weight. I share your concern about excess in the late Cărtărescu volumes, and I would not use it to dismiss him. You say you would weigh Adonis or Michon more heavily if the human dimension fails in the late books. I think that is the right fallback, and it is the same reason I now treat Adonis, not Can Xue, as my second alternative.

responses.point: Carlberg asks Palm which of Carson's works carry the whole-oeuvre case. She puts the formal-invention question as one of consistent literary architecture versus experiments, and she argues that the reshaping of a poetic language across decades is a claim about sustained achievement, not only invention.
responses.response: I agree that sustained achievement, and not invention alone, is the criterion. I have named the works I would test above. I do not think her case is a claim about a language in your sense. It is a claim about the recurring use of a classical inheritance to remake the relations between genres, and I think that is a form of sustained achievement. I accept that it is harder to establish than yours, and I hold it more tentatively than you hold Adonis. We agree that the citation scope matters. I would anchor mine in the verbal and narrative work and keep translation out of the credit.

uncertainties: My assessment of Carson rests on public knowledge of her major works and not on verified reading of the full corpus. The works I name as carrying the oeuvre case are not independently verified by me.
It is unresolved whether the breadth of her oeuvre matches the intensity of its best-known works. The through-line of method that I rely on is an argument and not a demonstration.
Hybrid and book-object works lose much in translation, so the committee's coverage would be uneven, and I weight the verbal and narrative work above them.

I cannot judge the Arabic prosody behind the Adonis case, Cărtărescu's late volumes, or whether Can Xue's method deepens over a large output. All comparisons across languages rest on uneven translation evidence.
The round-1 exchange did not settle the late-volume question for Cărtărescu, so my first alternative remains unconfirmed on the point that would move me.
Translation limits alone do not persuade me that no award (P000) is warranted. A recommendation should state its reliance on translations and secondary accounts openly.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My biographical work on Selma Lagerlöf, my collaboration with Kate Larson and my election alongside David Håkansson have no documented connection to Anne Carson, Mircea Cărtărescu, Adonis or any other shortlisted writer. My own literary practice is context and not evidence of a preference. Round 1 records that no member reports a connection to a leading candidate, and I have no new connection to disclose. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
